title: Karolinska eye-tracking classifier flags 9–10-year-olds at risk of persistent reading difficulty with 95.6% cross-validated accuracy (PLoS ONE 2016)
summary: A support-vector machine classifier from Karolinska Institutet identified 9–10-year-olds at risk of persistent reading difficulty from under one minute of eye tracking with 95.6% accuracy.
account: Mattias Nilsson Benfatto, Gustaf Öqvist Seimyr, Jan Ygge, Tony Pansell and Agneta Rydberg of Karolinska Institutet worked with Christer Jacobson of Linnaeus University. In PLoS ONE on 9 December 2016, they reported that eye-movement recordings of under one minute of reading can identify 9–10-year-olds at risk of persistent reading difficulties. They used cross-validation on 97 high-risk and 88 low-risk control subjects. A support-vector machine with recursive feature elimination selected 48 of 168 features. It reached 95.6% (± 4.5%) accuracy with balanced sensitivity and specificity. The competing-interests statement says that Benfatto and Seimyr own equity in Optolexia, a company aiming to offer technologies for assessing reading deficits in school-age children. The venture is funded by Sweden's innovation agency VINNOVA. The Ulla and Ingemar Dahlberg Foundation and the Promobilia Foundation also supported the work. The data are on Figshare. In August 2021 a team at the Slovak University of Technology reanalyzed the same 185 recordings with a different classifier and reported 96.6% accuracy, against 95.6% in the original paper. Lexplore, a Swedish company, sells a reading screener that it says Öqvist Seimyr and Nilsson Benfatto built on the Kronoberg data. The company's own site claims that one Swedish school group of 32 schools and 13,131 students used it from 2021/22 to 2024/25. Schools Week reported on 30 March 2025 that two English academy trusts had piloted Lexplore with 265 and 876 pupils. St Bart's Multi Academy Trust found that 226 of its 876 pupils in the baseline testing had below-average or worse reading ability. Schools Week also reported that a privacy group raised concerns about how pupils' data might be used.
purpose: The method was developed to screen for dyslexia risk from eye movements. The study reports the classification accuracy of that screen.

fields.summary: A support-vector machine classifier from Karolinska Institutet identified 9–10-year-olds at risk of persistent reading difficulty from under one minute of eye tracking with 95.6% accuracy.
fields.account: Mattias Nilsson Benfatto, Gustaf Öqvist Seimyr, Jan Ygge, Tony Pansell and Agneta Rydberg of Karolinska Institutet worked with Christer Jacobson of Linnaeus University. In PLoS ONE on 9 December 2016, they reported that eye-movement recordings of under one minute of reading can identify 9–10-year-olds at risk of persistent reading difficulties. They used cross-validation on 97 high-risk and 88 low-risk control subjects. A support-vector machine with recursive feature elimination selected 48 of 168 features. It reached 95.6% (± 4.5%) accuracy with balanced sensitivity and specificity. The competing-interests statement says that Benfatto and Seimyr own equity in Optolexia, a company aiming to offer technologies for assessing reading deficits in school-age children. The venture is funded by Sweden's innovation agency VINNOVA. The Ulla and Ingemar Dahlberg Foundation and the Promobilia Foundation also supported the work. The data are on Figshare. In August 2021 a team at the Slovak University of Technology reanalyzed the same 185 recordings with a different classifier and reported 96.6% accuracy, against 95.6% in the original paper. Lexplore, a Swedish company, sells a reading screener that it says Öqvist Seimyr and Nilsson Benfatto built on the Kronoberg data. The company's own site claims that one Swedish school group of 32 schools and 13,131 students used it from 2021/22 to 2024/25. Schools Week reported on 30 March 2025 that two English academy trusts had piloted Lexplore with 265 and 876 pupils. St Bart's Multi Academy Trust found that 226 of its 876 pupils in the baseline testing had below-average or worse reading ability. Schools Week also reported that a privacy group raised concerns about how pupils' data might be used.
